summary:
Canada is among the safest large destinations for trans visitors, and Nunavut stands directly under that national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Federal identity documents can carry an X marker, entry carries no trans-specific friction, and no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Nunavut adds its own statutory protection on top of the federal layer. Its Human Rights Act has listed gender identity and gender expression as protected grounds since 2017, when Nunavut MLAs voted unanimously on third and final reading of Bill 31. Justice Minister Keith Peterson said at the time that the amendment would make clear that discrimination against transgender people is prohibited. Nunavut was the first Canadian territory to enact such a provision; when it did, nine provinces and one territory already listed gender identity or expression in their human-rights laws.

Identity documents follow territorial statute. On 18 September 2025 Nunavut MLAs voted 12-8 in committee of the whole to restore a third non-binary sex-designation option on Nunavut birth certificates, amending the Vital Statistics Act after the standing committee had struck the option from Health Minister John Main's May 2025 bill; the bill was then approved on third reading. House leader Adam Arreak Lightstone said the Government of Nunavut now joins the rest of Canada in recognizing non-binary and transgender individuals.

Gender-affirming care in Nunavut is territorial and resident-facing rather than a visitor entitlement. Since March 2022 the Nunavut Health Department has funded transition-related care for transgender and non-binary residents, with breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty among the named procedures, under a partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal. Universal health coverage and the complaint route through the Canadian Human Rights Act apply nationally; detention remains the weakest part of the national framework, where placement according to gender identity and the withholding of gender-affirming care have both been contested in court.

No trans-specific incident series or policing pattern is on record for Nunavut itself. The available evidence is national in scope, and no metropolitan reporting hub exists in the territory, so local experience is poorly captured in official statistics.
tangentialFactors:
The national hate-crime climate runs alongside these protections. Statistics Canada recorded 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in 2024, up 1% after a 34% jump the previous year, for a rate of 11.9 per 100,000; across the longer arc police-reported hate crime has risen for six consecutive years and is up 169% since 2018. Incidents motivated by gender identity and gender expression rose 8% to 139 in 2024, a fourth consecutive annual increase and a 184% rise since 2020, making that category among the fastest-growing.

Incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, ending three consecutive years of increases from a 2023 peak of 889, though June 2024 alone recorded 113 incidents against a monthly average of roughly 50. Metropolitan areas record rates about 2.5 times higher than smaller towns; Nunavut has no metropolitan reporting hub, so the higher-intensity pattern documented for large cities does not map onto the territory's population centres.

Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report works through police-reported data including gender identity and expression motivations and supplies national 2SLGBTQ+ victimisation context rather than territorial figures; the organisation also documents an increasingly organised anti-trans movement.

Two provinces have moved in the opposite direction. Alberta and Saskatchewan have enacted policy rollbacks affecting trans people living there, including school-facing measures on names, pronouns and notification of parents. These rules govern residents of those provinces rather than visitors, but they mark the direction of provincial politics running alongside the human-rights statutes.
localsOnly:
Transition-related care for transgender and non-binary residents has been funded by the Nunavut Health Department since March 2022. The named procedures are breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty, delivered under a partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal.

The local LGBTQ group Positive Space called the funding overdue while flagging information gaps for residents living outside Iqaluit, the territorial capital. Those gaps, and how residents outside the capital are referred to and travel for surgery, are not addressed in the reporting.

The Human Rights Act protection added in 2017 covers residents as well as visitors, and discrimination complaints have a defined route through the territory's human-rights process alongside the federal one. The restored non-binary sex designation on birth certificates applies to Nunavut-issued vital-statistics documents, which govern residents' standing records rather than travel documents.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific incident series, policing pattern or territorial hate-crime breakdown is on record for Nunavut, and no metropolitan reporting hub exists in the territory, so local experience here is poorly captured in official data. The Statistics Canada and Egale Canada material is national and cannot be read as Nunavut figures; whether territorial under-reporting is material is unresolved and not sourced.

The restored third sex-designation option on Nunavut birth certificates is sourced to the September 2025 committee vote and third reading of the amended Vital Statistics Act. Whether the option is now being issued, what supporting documentation is required, and how long processing takes are unresolved and not sourced here.

Coverage of gender-affirming care is documented for residents under the territorial health budget. Whether a visitor, newcomer or non-resident is eligible, what wait times apply, and how travel to the partner surgical centre is arranged are unresolved and not sourced. Positive Space's flagged information gaps outside the capital remain open in the reporting available.
